title: WildChat: 1M ChatGPT Interaction Logs in the Wild
author_note: Wenting Zhao and Yuntian Deng contributed equally.
date_note: First arXiv version, following the ICLR submission and initial dataset release.
dataset_version: The original paper's approximately one-million-conversation release; some experiments use earlier collection windows.
summary: Introduces consented, multilingual, multi-turn conversations with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, together with timestamps and metadata for studying use across time and locations. The paper examines language and prompt diversity, toxicity and jailbreaks, and instruction tuning with WildLlama.
finding: WildChat covers 68 languages with more than 100 user prompts each. The paper demonstrates instruction tuning with a Llama-2 7B model.
evidence_note: Sections 2–5: collection, language coverage, safety analyses, and WildLlama.
citation_title: WildChat: 1M ChatGPT Interaction Logs in the Wild
container_title: International Conference on Learning Representations

title: WildVis: Open Source Visualizer for Million-Scale Chat Logs in the Wild
dataset_version: Approximately one million WildChat conversations, alongside LMSYS-Chat-1M.
summary: Provides search filters and an embedding map for exploring WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M. Its case studies connect individual conversations to broader topic patterns and reproduce examples from research on journalism and personal disclosures.
finding: The visual comparison identifies a Midjourney prompt-generation cluster in WildChat and a chemistry cluster in LMSYS-Chat-1M.
evidence_note: Sections 2–4: interface, indexed datasets, and case studies. Appendix E: cross-dataset comparison.
citation_title: WildVis: Open Source Visualizer for Million-Scale Chat Logs in the Wild
container_title: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations

title: WildBench: Benchmarking LLMs with Challenging Tasks from Real Users in the Wild
date_note: First arXiv version; the paper also describes benchmark releases in March and May 2024.
dataset_version: WildBench V2: 1,024 tasks curated from WildChat collection data and held out of the public WildChat training corpus.
summary: Turns challenging user requests from WildChat into an evaluation set with task-specific checklists. The selection process combines language and quality filters, model difficulty estimates, and manual review. Selected conversations are held out of the public WildChat release.
finding: For the top-ranked models evaluated in the paper, WB-Reward has a Pearson correlation of 0.98 with Chatbot Arena's human-voted Elo ratings.
evidence_note: Section 2.1: selection and held-out data. Sections 3–4: metrics and model rankings.
citation_title: WildBench: Benchmarking LLMs with Challenging Tasks from Real Users in the Wild

title: Trust No Bot: Discovering Personal Disclosures in Human-LLM Conversations in the Wild
dataset_version: A 5,000-conversation English sample from the one-million-conversation WildChat corpus, limited to one conversation per hashed IP with additional prefix and length filters.
summary: Studies the tasks and contexts in which people disclose personal or sensitive information to chatbots. It combines automated PII detection with task and sensitive-topic taxonomies, releasing annotations that support analyses beyond conventional identifiers.
finding: Sensitive disclosures in the analyzed sample include preferences, personal habits, and application-related information that conventional PII detectors miss.
evidence_note: Section 2: sampling. Sections 3–4: detected identifiers and sensitive topics.
citation_title: Trust No Bot: Discovering Personal Disclosures in Human-LLM Conversations in the Wild
citation_note: 2024 arXiv preprint; also published at COLM 2024.

title: Developing Story: Case Studies of Generative AI's Use in Journalism
date_note: First arXiv version, initially titled Breaking News; the revised title is Developing Story.
dataset_version: An earlier WildChat release containing approximately 650,000 conversations.
summary: Matches conversations in WildChat to published articles from two news agencies, documenting how source material and generated drafts enter journalistic workflows. The study examines input materials, overlap with published text, and publication timing.
finding: The authors match 78 conversations to 111 published articles and report a median output-to-publication ROUGE-L overlap of 0.62.
evidence_note: Section 2: dataset release. Table 1: matched conversations and articles. Section 3: text overlap.
citation_title: Developing Story: Case Studies of Generative AI's Use in Journalism
citation_note: 2024 arXiv preprint under its revised title, Developing Story; also published at SoLaR 2024.

title: WildChat-50M: A Deep Dive Into the Role of Synthetic Data in Post-Training
dataset_version: A synthetic-response extension of WildChat-1M, retaining its user prompts and adding responses from open-weight models.
summary: Uses WildChat prompts to compare responses from more than 50 open-weight model checkpoints and study the choice of synthetic-data generator. The authors also construct Re-Wild, a supervised fine-tuning mixture, and test it with Llama-3.1 8B.
finding: Re-Wild outperforms the Tulu-3 SFT mixture on the paper’s aggregate evaluations using 40% as many training samples.
evidence_note: Section 2: WildChat-1M prompts and 54 model checkpoints. Section 3: SFT mixtures and evaluations.
citation_title: WildChat-50M: A Deep Dive Into the Role of Synthetic Data in Post-Training
container_title: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning

title: WildClaims: Conversational Information Access in the Wild(Chat)
date_note: First arXiv version; the ECIR 2026 paper uses the revised title shown here.
dataset_version: 3,000 sampled English WildChat conversations after excluding math and coding.
summary: Examines factual information conveyed by chatbot responses, including when the user's main task is editing or creative writing. It releases extracted claims and check-worthiness annotations to study information access beyond explicit questions.
finding: WildClaims contains 121,905 extracted claims from 7,587 assistant utterances; estimated check-worthy-conversation prevalence varies substantially with the annotation method.
evidence_note: Section 3 and Table 2: selection and annotation counts. The prevalence analysis compares classification methods.
citation_title: WildClaims: Conversational Information Access in the Wild(Chat)
container_title: Advances in Information Retrieval. ECIR 2026
citation_note: ECIR 2026 proceedings paper under its revised title; first posted as a preprint in September 2025.

title: Adopt ≠ Adapt: Longitudinal Analyses of LLM Conversations in the Wild
date_note: First arXiv version; annotation follows the August 2026 revision.
dataset_version: WildChat-4.8M, with hashed-IP filters and a main-analysis cutoff before September 2024 to reduce later API-like activity.
summary: Compares individual and population-level usage patterns in Bing Copilot and WildChat-4.8M. The study tracks changes over a user’s history and compares users with different activity levels across the two platforms.
finding: WildChat users’ intent and domain distributions more closely resemble high-activity Copilot users than low-activity users.
evidence_note: Section 3.2: hashed-IP filters and time cutoff. Section 6 and Figure 6: activity groups across the two sources.
citation_title: Adopt ≠ Adapt: Longitudinal Analyses of LLM Conversations in the Wild

title: AI Fiction in the Wild
date_note: First arXiv version; presented earlier at the MFS Cultural AI Conference on September 19, 2025.
dataset_version: 573,453 English-language conversations from the first WildChat release, covering April 2023–May 2024.
summary: Studies how people generate and consume fiction through chatbots, combining conversation classification with close reading of repeated story requests. The authors examine fanfiction, roleplay, and erotic fiction, and discuss how iterative generation can reshape the relationship between reader and writer. A companion viewer supports exploration of the fiction subset.
finding: The study classifies 195,271 conversations (34%) as fiction. Sampling one conversation per inferred user reduces this share to 7.1%.
evidence_note: Sections 3–4: classification and user grouping by hashed IPs and similar prompts. Table 3: conversation counts.
citation_title: AI Fiction in the Wild

title: The Garden of Forking Prompts: How Users Explore Narrative Space in Story Generation
dataset_version: The yuntian-deng/WildChat-4.8M-Full release, filtered to 2,560,447 English prompt-response pairs with prompts of at least 20 words; one story-shape analysis uses WildChat-1M.
summary: Introduces WildStories, containing 275,635 story prompts, and WildEdits, containing 24,291 reconstructed edit trees. The study follows revisions across separate conversations, organizes edits by direction and narrative target, and uses this framework to generate story-prompt variations for evaluation.
finding: 94.2% of prompts with an identified parent link to a different WildChat conversation, showing how story revisions span separate conversations.
evidence_note: Sections 3–4: sampling, inferred users, and edit-tree construction. Sections 5–6: revisions and prompt permutation.
citation_title: The Garden of Forking Prompts: How Users Explore Narrative Space in Story Generation
container_title: Third Conference on Language Modeling

title: Speak Easy: Eliciting Harmful Jailbreaks from LLMs with Simple Interactions
dataset_version: Real-world conversations retrieved through WildVis motivate the study. Experiments use HarmBench, AdvBench, SORRY-Bench, and MedSafetyBench.
summary: Uses conversations found through WildVis to study safety failures during multi-step and multilingual interactions. The paper introduces HarmScore to assess the actionability and informativeness of harmful responses, and tests these interaction patterns across four safety benchmarks.
finding: Figure 2 uses WildVis conversations to illustrate the interaction patterns tested in the safety evaluation.
evidence_note: Section 4 and Figure 2: WildVis conversations. Section 5: benchmark evaluation.
citation_title: Speak Easy: Eliciting Harmful Jailbreaks from LLMs with Simple Interactions
container_title: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning

title: A corpus-based analysis of politeness strategies in Arabic speakers’ interactions with ChatGPT
dataset_version: 349 Arabic-dominant WildChat conversations with at least ten turns, retrieved through WildVis.
summary: Examines user-side politeness in Arabic conversations selected through WildVis. The authors code prompts with an adapted Brown and Levinson framework and compare openings, conversation bodies, closings, and topic shifts to study directness and relational language in human–AI interaction.
finding: Bald on-record strategies account for 88.42% of coded instances in the selected conversations.
evidence_note: Sections 3.1–3.2: WildVis retrieval and coding. Section 4.1: strategy proportions.
citation_title: A corpus-based analysis of politeness strategies in Arabic speakers’ interactions with ChatGPT
container_title: Cogent Arts & Humanities

title: Prevalence of Mental Health Discussions in Publicly Available Generative AI Conversations
dataset_version: 620,699 conversations from WildChat-4.8M.
summary: Studies how the definition of a mental-health conversation changes prevalence estimates in WildChat-4.8M. A classifier scores topicality, help-seeking intent, clinical language, and affective risk, with validation against independently coded conversations.
finding: The estimated share of mental-health conversations is 0.21% when the definition requires explicit help-seeking for an identifiable person, and 4.90% when any mental-health topicality qualifies.
evidence_note: Methods: corpus, four classification domains, and 370-conversation validation sample. Results: comparison of definitions.
citation_title: Prevalence of Mental Health Discussions in Publicly Available Generative AI Conversations
container_title: JAMA Network Open

title: RewardBench 2: Advancing Reward Model Evaluation
dataset_version: Previously unreleased WildChat prompts supply approximately 70% of the 1,865-prompt benchmark.
summary: Builds a reward-model benchmark around previously unseen human prompts from WildChat, combining quality and topic filtering with manual verification. It evaluates reward models across factuality, precise instruction following, math, safety, focus, and ties, and studies how benchmark scores relate to best-of-N sampling and RLHF.
finding: WildChat supplies the human-prompt domains: factuality (475), precise instruction following (160), math (183), and focus (495). The safety and ties domains use other prompt sources.
evidence_note: Section 3 and Table 2: WildChat prompts and benchmark composition. Sections 4–5: reward models and downstream use.
citation_title: RewardBench 2: Advancing Reward Model Evaluation

title: From Chat Logs to Collective Insights: Aggregative Question Answering
dataset_version: A filtered WildChat-Full release of roughly 990,000 conversations, reduced to 182,330 conversations after deduplication, length limits, and an active-user requirement.
summary: Introduces aggregative question answering: answering questions that require combining evidence across many conversations. WildChat-AQA pairs conversation text and metadata with inferred topics and keywords, and compares retrieval, fine-tuning, and the PROBE retrieval method.
finding: The benchmark contains 6,027 questions over 182,330 conversations. PROBE improves over standard retrieval, with retrieval and reasoning errors remaining in the evaluated systems.
evidence_note: Section 2 and Appendix E: construction, model-generated questions, and human quality checks. Section 4: ranking quality, retrieval, and computational cost.
citation_title: From Chat Logs to Collective Insights: Aggregative Question Answering
container_title: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

title: Prototypical Human-AI Collaboration Behaviors from LLM-Assisted Writing in the Wild
dataset_version: Approximately 68,000 English writing sessions from WildChat-1M, filtered to at least two user utterances; compared with writing sessions from Bing Copilot.
summary: Studies how users steer writing across successive turns. The authors label follow-up types, identify recurring collaboration patterns with principal component analysis, and relate those patterns to writing intents such as brainstorming, technical drafting, and long-form composition.
finding: Seven collaboration patterns account for 80–85% of the variance in the analyzed follow-up representations; explicit positive or negative feedback appears in only a small minority of sessions.
evidence_note: Sections 3–6 and Appendix B: WildChat subset, analysis, and shared patterns across the two services.
citation_title: Prototypical Human-AI Collaboration Behaviors from LLM-Assisted Writing in the Wild
container_title: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

title: Navigating Rifts in Human-LLM Grounding: Study and Benchmark
dataset_version: Non-toxic English WildChat conversations, sampled at one conversation per user for the main grounding analysis; RIFTS selects initial prompts from WildChat.
summary: Analyzes how users and assistants establish mutual understanding, alongside Bing Chat and human-human MultiWOZ conversations. It releases grounding annotations, a forecasting approach, and RIFTS to test when assistants should clarify, ask follow-up questions, or proceed.
finding: RIFTS contains 1,740 tasks. The evaluated assistants rarely take useful grounding initiative; forecasting-based prompting improves their performance.
evidence_note: Section 4: data filters. Section 6 and Appendix A: benchmark construction and evaluation.
citation_title: Navigating Rifts in Human-LLM Grounding: Study and Benchmark
container_title: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)

title: WildFeedback: Aligning LLMs With In-situ User Interactions And Feedback
dataset_version: 148,715 multi-turn conversations from the original WildChat corpus, used to identify feedback and construct 20,281 preference examples.
summary: Converts naturally occurring user feedback into preferred and dispreferred responses. Its pipeline detects satisfaction and dissatisfaction, constructs preference examples, and evaluates responses against checklists derived from the feedback.
finding: WildFeedback contains 20,281 preference examples. Fine-tuned models improve on the paper’s alignment and checklist-based evaluations.
evidence_note: Sections 2–3: feedback mining and evaluation. Appendix E: WildChat source.
citation_title: WildFeedback: Aligning LLMs With In-situ User Interactions And Feedback
container_title: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)

title: User Feedback in Human-LLM Dialogues: A Lens to Understand Users But Noisy as a Learning Signal
dataset_version: WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M, including dense manual annotations on 34 WildChat conversations and separate 1,000-conversation samples for feedback-conditioned response experiments.
summary: Examines the frequency, meaning, and usefulness of implicit feedback in real conversations. It separates feedback polarity from what users actually request, and tests whether regenerating responses with that additional context improves model training.
finding: Feedback semantics help on MTBench but do not consistently improve the longer, more complex WildBench tasks; positive feedback alone can be a noisy training signal.
evidence_note: Sections 3–4: manual labels and user behavior. Sections 5–7: regeneration and training. Table 1: the 34-conversation WildChat annotation sample.
citation_title: User Feedback in Human-LLM Dialogues: A Lens to Understand Users But Noisy as a Learning Signal
container_title: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

title: Show or Tell? Modeling the evolution of request-making in Human-LLM conversations
dataset_version: 211,414 English request-making first turns from 18,964 inferred users, drawn from WildChat conversations collected between April 2023 and May 2024.
summary: Introduces ReCCRE, which separates request content, context, assigned roles, and general expressions in user prompts. The study tracks how users phrase requests as they gain experience and over calendar time.
finding: Users include more context in their requests over time, and individual users’ expression patterns tend to stabilize with experience.
evidence_note: Sections 3–5: segmentation, filtering, and longitudinal analyses.
citation_title: Show or Tell? Modeling the evolution of request-making in Human-LLM conversations
container_title: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2026

title: Invisible failures in human-AI interactions
dataset_version: 100,000 filtered English conversations from the original WildChat corpus, plus counterfactual model responses to 2,000 sampled single-turn conversations.
summary: Develops a taxonomy of eight failure patterns that may occur without an explicit user complaint. The authors use model-assisted annotations with human oversight to analyze failures and compare original responses with newer models on a sampled set of prompts.
finding: Among conversations labeled as failures in the annotated sample, 79% were invisible: the user gave no overt signal of the problem.
evidence_note: Sections 3–4: sampling and annotation. Section 5: replacement responses from newer models.
citation_title: Invisible failures in human-AI interactions

title: A paradox of AI fluency
dataset_version: 27,000 English transcripts sampled across 27 months from the non-toxic WildChat-4.8M release, with separate analyses of recurring Midjourney and Blockman interaction clusters.
summary: Relates inferred AI fluency to task complexity and conversational outcomes. The study compares active iteration, critical evaluation, and passive acceptance, and examines how these behaviors relate to visible and invisible failures.
finding: More fluent users attempt harder tasks and show more visible failures, yet achieve greater success on complex work; less fluent users more often have failures without overt negative feedback.
evidence_note: Sections 3–5: monthly sampling, cluster handling, model-assisted annotation, and outcome analysis.
citation_title: A paradox of AI fluency

title: WildReward: Learning Reward Models from In-the-Wild Human Interactions
dataset_version: Filtered English and Chinese conversations from WildChat-4.8M, yielding approximately 186,000 feedback instances for the WildFB training data.
summary: Trains reward models directly on implicit user feedback using ordinal regression. Its pipeline classifies feedback, filters ambiguous signals, and validates refusal cases before training; experiments examine calibration, cross-prompt score consistency, user diversity, and online DPO.
finding: Broader user diversity improves reward modeling. WildReward models also improve online DPO results over the reward-model baseline tested in the paper.
evidence_note: Section 2: mining and training. Section 4: score consistency and user diversity. Appendix A: WildChat-4.8M language and quality filters.
citation_title: WildReward: Learning Reward Models from In-the-Wild Human Interactions
container_title: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)

title: WildTeaming at Scale: From In-the-Wild Jailbreaks to (Adversarially) Safer Language Models
dataset_version: Single-turn WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M examples filtered for potentially harmful interactions; WildChat contributes 8,981 adversarial queries to the tactic inventory.
summary: Mines naturally occurring jailbreak tactics and combines them into adversarial tests and synthetic safety-training examples. The resulting WildJailbreak resource contains harmful and benign requests in both direct and adversarial forms, enabling experiments on safety and over-refusal.
finding: WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M yield 5,688 tactic clusters. The synthetic WildJailbreak dataset contains approximately 262,000 prompt-response pairs.
evidence_note: Section 2 and Table 1: WildChat and LMSYS contributions. Sections 4–5: WildJailbreak and safety-training experiments.
citation_title: WildTeaming at Scale: From In-the-Wild Jailbreaks to (Adversarially) Safer Language Models
container_title: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems

title: WildGuard: Open One-Stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs
dataset_version: WildChat prompts form one component of a mixed-source moderation dataset; additional sources include LMSYS, annotator-written safety data, and synthetic adversarial examples.
summary: Builds a moderation model that jointly identifies harmful requests, harmful responses, and refusals. WildChat contributes real user prompts and, through the WildTeaming pipeline, observed jailbreak tactics used to construct adversarial examples.
finding: WildGuardMix contains roughly 92,000 examples, including a 5,299-item human-annotated test set. The resource supports both safety evaluation and moderation-model training.
evidence_note: Section 3.1: WildChat sampling and tactic-based generation. Section 3.2: test annotation.
citation_title: WildGuard: Open One-Stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs
container_title: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems

title: WildCode Revisited: A Comprehensive Empirical Study on the Security of LLM-Generated Code
date_note: First arXiv version, originally titled WildCode: An Empirical Analysis of Code Generated by ChatGPT.
dataset_version: 82,843 conversations containing generated code from an 837,989-conversation WildChat release; user-intent analyses use a filtered English subset of 34,478 conversations.
summary: Examines the security and quality of code generated in real user interactions, together with user intent and follow-up behavior. The extended study also tests security-oriented prompting strategies using prompts derived from the observed logs.
finding: Security concerns are uncommon in the analyzed user requests, even when generated code has detected problems.
evidence_note: Section 3: extraction and language filtering. Sections 4–6: code, prompting, and user intent.
citation_title: WildCode Revisited: A Comprehensive Empirical Study on the Security of LLM-Generated Code
citation_note: 2025 arXiv preprint, extended June 2026 revision with updated title and author list.

title: “An bhfuil Gaeilge agat?”: Differences in User Interaction and Assistant Responses Across Languages of European Origin in Large-scale Conversational Datasets
date_note: CEUR proceedings publication date; presented at AICS 2024 on December 9–10, 2024.
dataset_version: WildChat (990,372 conversations) combined with LMSYS-Chat-1M; language and quality filters leave 781,376 conversations across 28 languages of European origin.
summary: Compares topics, conversation length, sentiment, moderation scores, and inferred satisfaction across 28 languages using WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M. The study combines corpus analysis with a classifier for user–assistant–user interaction triples.
finding: Topics substantially overlap across language groups, while conversation length and moderation scores vary. A model estimates satisfaction from user–assistant–user interaction triples.
evidence_note: Section 2: dataset combination and filtering. Sections 3–7: topic, length, sentiment, moderation, and satisfaction analyses.
citation_title: “An bhfuil Gaeilge agat?”: Differences in User Interaction and Assistant Responses Across Languages of European Origin in Large-scale Conversational Datasets
container_title: Proceedings of the 32nd Irish Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Science
citation_note: The conference took place in December 2024; CEUR published volume 3910 in March 2025.

title: Trust Me, I’m Wrong: LLMs Hallucinate with Certainty Despite Knowing the Answer
citation_title: Trust Me, I’m Wrong: LLMs Hallucinate with Certainty Despite Knowing the Answer
container_title: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025
dataset_version: Queries WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M through WildVis to validate help-seeking prompt styles; the main experiments use Natural Questions and TriviaQA.
summary: Uses WildVis to check that prompt variations in a hallucination study resemble real human requests. The paper studies cases where models give confident incorrect answers after small prompt changes despite consistently answering the original question correctly.
finding: The authors use WildVis searches and WildChat examples to validate the help-seeking language used in their evaluation prompts.
evidence_note: Section 3.1: prompt construction and validation. Appendix F.2: WildVis searches of WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M.

title: SeaExam and SeaBench: Benchmarking LLMs with Local Multilingual Questions in Southeast Asia
citation_title: SeaExam and SeaBench: Benchmarking LLMs with Local Multilingual Questions in Southeast Asia
container_title: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2025
dataset_version: Wild Queries combines filtered WildChat-1M and LMSYS-Chat-1M inputs in Indonesian, Thai, and Vietnamese; the paper reports 4,658 queries across the two sources.
summary: Builds Southeast Asian evaluation sets from local sources and uses real conversations to test how closely they reflect everyday requests. WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M supply the Wild Queries comparison corpus after language checks, length limits, and filtering.
finding: In embedding-based comparisons, the locally constructed SeaExam and SeaBench are closer to the observed query distribution than translated MMLU and MT-Bench.
evidence_note: Section 3.1: Wild Queries construction and distribution comparisons. Appendix B and Table 10: language breakdown.

title: JailbreakHunter: A Visual Analytics Approach for Jailbreak Prompts Discovery From Large-Scale Human-LLM Conversational Datasets
date_note: First arXiv version; the journal article appeared online in April 2025 and in the October 2025 issue.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
dataset_version: An earlier WildChat release containing more than 500,000 conversations, alongside LMSYS-Chat-1M.
summary: Provides visual analysis at the group, conversation, and individual-turn levels to find jailbreak attempts in conversation logs. Analysts combine filtering, cluster views, conversation timelines, and comparisons with previously reported prompts; a case study uses WildChat to investigate multi-turn attempts after an initial model refusal.
finding: The WildChat case study filters for multi-turn interactions and moderation scores to narrow the search to 503 conversations. Evaluation includes two case studies and interviews with nine researchers.
evidence_note: Section III-C: datasets. Section VI-B: WildChat case study and filters. Section VI-C: expert evaluation.
citation_title: JailbreakHunter: A Visual Analytics Approach for Jailbreak Prompts Discovery From Large-Scale Human-LLM Conversational Datasets
container_title: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
citation_note: 2025 journal article; the annotations use the July 2024 preprint.

title: Quantifying the Utility of User Simulators for Building Collaborative LLM Assistants
dataset_version: WildChat-1M provides human utterances for user-simulator training; WildChat-4.8M and WildBench support evaluation and tests of generalization.
summary: Tests whether learning a user simulator from real conversations helps train assistants that work better with people. The study fine-tunes simulators on WildChat user utterances, trains assistants through simulated interaction, and evaluates them on WildBench and in a study with 283 participants.
finding: The assistant trained with the learned user simulator wins 58% of comparisons against the initial assistant in the human study; training with a role-playing model yields 51%.
evidence_note: Sections 2–3 and Appendix C: WildChat preprocessing and simulator training. Section 5: human study.
citation_title: Quantifying the Utility of User Simulators for Building Collaborative LLM Assistants

title: A Course Correction in Steerability Evaluation: Revealing Miscalibration and Side Effects in LLMs
dataset_version: English-language examples retrieved through WildVis validate the study’s text-rewriting goals; the controlled experiments use separate source-text corpora.
summary: Uses keyword searches and manual review in WildVis to select realistic goals for text rewriting. The study tests whether models can change one property, such as reading difficulty or formality, while controlling other properties.
finding: WildVis examples support the choice of rewriting goals. The experiments find miscalibration and unintended changes to other text properties.
evidence_note: Appendix D.5: WildVis searches, English filtering, manual review, and conversation examples.
citation_title: A Course Correction in Steerability Evaluation: Revealing Miscalibration and Side Effects in LLMs
container_title: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
